431.event_title: Louis IX hears his subjects' cases himself at Vincennes
431.event: King Louis IX of France often administered justice in person, and his companion and biographer Jean de Joinville recorded that at Vincennes, after Mass, the king would sit in the open and let anyone with a dispute approach him directly, without ushers in the way. From 1247 he sent out commissions of inquiry to hear complaints against his own royal officials. His reputation for fairness was so great that foreign rulers asked him to arbitrate their disputes, and he was canonised in 1297.
431.explanation: Louis IX's power and wealth were remembered not as a cause for fear but as a source of honour, because he used them with restraint and approachability.
431.tie_back: The kural says prosperity has real dignity only when free of arrogance, anger and base desire, and Louis IX's open, patient justice gave his greatness that dignity.
431._accuracy_note: Shows a ruler honoured for restraint and fairness, but the sources document his justice and piety more than the specific absence of all three faults the kural names.

432.event_title: King Farouk of Egypt is forced to abdicate
432.event: King Farouk, who came to the throne of Egypt in 1936, became known for a self-indulgent lifestyle, lavish spending and expensive shopping trips abroad, while the army was angered by defeat in the 1948 war and by reports that the king's associates had profited from supplying faulty weapons. On 23 July 1952 the Free Officers, led by Muhammad Naguib and Gamal Abdel Nasser, seized power. Surrounded at Ras el-Tin palace in Alexandria, Farouk abdicated on 26 July in favour of his infant son and sailed into exile; the monarchy was abolished the following year.
432.explanation: Farouk's personal excesses steadily destroyed the loyalty and respect on which his throne rested.
432.tie_back: The kural warns that avarice, false pride and delight in unworthy things are the faults that harm a ruler, and Farouk's indulgence cost him his crown.
432._accuracy_note: A clear case of unworthy pleasures harming a ruler; the sources stress extravagance more than avarice, so the kural's triad is matched only in part.

433.event_title: Hugh Dalton resigns over a budget leak
433.place: Palace of Westminster, London, United Kingdom
433.event: On his way into the House of Commons to deliver his budget, Chancellor of the Exchequer Hugh Dalton stopped to talk with a lobby journalist and mentioned some of his tax plans. The journalist's evening paper printed them shortly before Dalton reached that part of his speech. Although the slip was brief and had little practical effect, Dalton apologised to the House and offered his resignation, which Prime Minister Clement Attlee accepted the next day.
433.explanation: Dalton treated a small indiscretion as a grave breach of his duty to Parliament and gave up one of the highest offices in government because of it.
433.tie_back: The kural says those who dread disgrace treat a fault as small as a millet seed as if it were as tall as a palmyra palm, and Dalton resigned over a few leaked lines.
433._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's scale contrast between a tiny fault and a huge response, though sources note political pressure as well as conscience behind the resignation.

434.event_title: Sakichi Toyoda builds looms that stop themselves at the first fault
434.event: In 1896 the inventor Sakichi Toyoda produced a power loom with a device that automatically stopped the machine when a weft thread broke, so that it would not go on weaving defective cloth. His Type G automatic loom of 1924 included stopping devices for broken warp or weft threads among its many automatic mechanisms. Toyota later named this principle jidoka, stopping immediately when an abnormality is detected, and made it one of the two pillars of the Toyota Production System.
434.explanation: Toyoda's idea was that a fault caught at once costs little, while a fault left running multiplies into waste, and the principle became central to modern quality control.
434.tie_back: The kural tells us to make guarding against faults our chief aim because fault itself is the enemy, and Toyoda built that vigilance into the very machine.
434._accuracy_note: A precise mechanical picture of treating faults as the real enemy, though it concerns manufacturing defects rather than the moral faults of a ruler.

435.event_title: The Chernobyl reactor explodes during a safety test
435.place: Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, near Pripyat, Soviet Union (now Ukraine)
435.event: Early on 26 April 1986, operators at Unit 4 of the Chernobyl plant were running a test, and a series of actions, including disabling automatic shutdown systems, left the reactor in an extremely unstable state. When they tried to shut it down, a design flaw in the control rods caused a sudden power surge, and explosions and fire destroyed the reactor and released large amounts of radioactive material. Later reviews named major design deficiencies, violations of operating procedures and the absence of a safety culture as causes, and many thousands of people had to leave their homes.
435.explanation: Known weaknesses and lax procedures, left uncorrected beforehand, turned a routine test into one of the worst industrial disasters in history within seconds.
435.tie_back: The kural warns that one who does not guard against faults before they arrive will be destroyed like a heap of straw before a fire, and Chernobyl's unaddressed flaws ended in literal fire.
435._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the cost of failing to prevent faults in advance, though the kural speaks of a person's life and character rather than an institution's safety system.

436.event_title: Pope John Paul II's Day of Pardon
436.event: On the first Sunday of Lent in the Jubilee year 2000, Pope John Paul II led a service in St Peter's Basilica in which senior cardinals and bishops confessed categories of sins committed by members of the Catholic Church over the centuries. These included divisions among Christians, the use of violence in the service of truth, hostility toward followers of other religions including Jews, and wrongs against women, the poor and minorities. After each confession the pope asked God's forgiveness.
436.explanation: The ceremony was an unprecedented public act by a major institution examining and confessing its own past faults before addressing those of others.
436.tie_back: The kural says a ruler who first removes his own faults and only then examines others' will be free of fault, and the Day of Pardon began with the Church's own record.
436._accuracy_note: Shows self-scrutiny placed before judgement of others, but it was an act of confession for an institution's past rather than a ruler's personal programme of reform.

437.event_title: Nadir Shah carries off the Mughal treasury and the Peacock Throne
437.event: In 1739 the Persian ruler Nadir Shah defeated the larger army of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah at Karnal and then entered Delhi. He took away the Mughal treasury and the jewelled Peacock Throne built for Shah Jahan, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond most likely formed part of the plunder. The loss left the Mughal treasury depleted and the empire greatly weakened.
437.explanation: Wealth that had been gathered and stored over generations did nothing to protect the empire and was lost to another in a matter of weeks.
437.tie_back: The kural says the wealth of one who will not put it to its proper use does not endure but perishes without benefit, and the Mughal hoard passed to a foreign conqueror.
437._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the treasure was indeed lost without benefit, but the sources do not document Muhammad Shah as a miser, so the kural's moral cause is not shown.

438.event_title: Emperor Galba refuses the soldiers' promised reward
438.event: Servius Sulpicius Galba became Roman emperor in 68 CE after the fall of Nero, and Suetonius describes his reputation for stinginess. He refused to pay the Praetorian Guard the donative, a cash reward, that had been promised in his name, and he passed over his ally Otho to name another man as his heir. Otho won the guard over with a promise of payment, and on 15 January 69 the praetorians killed Galba in the Roman Forum after a reign of about seven months.
438.explanation: Galba's tight grip on money turned the very soldiers who should have protected him into the instrument of his fall.
438.tie_back: The kural calls a grasping heart a fault beyond all others, and Galba's refusal to part with what he owed undid every other strength he had as emperor.
438._accuracy_note: A clear case of miserliness ruining a ruler; modern historians also stress political misjudgement, so avarice was one cause among several.

439.event: Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who had ruled the Central African Republic since 1966, renamed it the Central African Empire and in December 1977 crowned himself emperor in a lavish ceremony. The event cost more than 20 million dollars, financed largely by France, in one of the world's poorest countries. Bokassa was overthrown in September 1979 in a coup backed by France.
439.explanation: The coronation became a byword for a ruler's self-glorification at his people's expense, and it brought him ridicule rather than respect.
439.tie_back: The kural forbids a ruler to admire himself or to desire deeds that bring no good, and Bokassa's coronation was both at once.
439._accuracy_note: Nearly a dramatisation of both prohibitions in the kural, self-admiration and a costly, useless deed.

440.event_title: Henry Kissinger's secret journey to Beijing
440.event: During an official visit to Pakistan in July 1971, United States National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger let it be known that he was unwell and resting at a hill resort, while in fact he flew secretly from Pakistan to Beijing. There he held long talks with Premier Zhou Enlai to prepare a visit by President Richard Nixon. The trip stayed hidden until 15 July, when both governments announced Nixon's planned visit to China.
440.explanation: Because the American aim was kept from rivals and from the press until it was achieved, no one had the chance to obstruct the opening to China before it happened.
440.tie_back: The kural says that if one can pursue what one desires without others knowing, the schemes of rivals come to nothing, and Kissinger's concealed journey achieved its goal unopposed.
440._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows the strategic value of concealing one's aims, but the kural is about hiding a ruler's personal desires and appetites, which this does not involve.
